2224A - Zhily and Array Operating
We want to maximize every single number so that the final goodness is the best.

An operation at $$$i$$$ only changes $$$a_i$$$; it never harms positivity elsewhere, but may make $$$a_j$$$ bigger for $$$j \lt i$$$.So we greedily judge every $$$i=n-1$$$ down to $$$1$$$. If $$$a_{i+1} \gt 0$$$, adding it strictly increases, increasing the chance of having more positives. Otherwise, adding it would not help, so we skip it.
2224B - Zhily and Mex and Max
2224B - Zhily and Mex and Max
First, we demonstrate that the maximum element ($$$max$$$) must be placed in the first position. After that, we can put the smallest number that does not appear in the new array to maximize the mex.
Suppose this is not the case, and $$$max$$$ first appears at index $$$i+1$$$. Let $$$t$$$ be the MEX of the first $$$i$$$ positions; it follows that $$$t \leq i$$$.

If we move $$$max$$$ directly to the first position (shifting the original elements one step back), consider the changes in the first $$$i$$$ prefix sets (the sets from position $$$i+1$$$ onwards remain unchanged):
Contribution of prefix maximums: The sum increases by at least $$$i$$$, as the original maximum for each of the first $$$i$$$ prefixes was strictly less than $$$max$$$.

Contribution of prefix MEX: The sum decreases by at most $$$t$$$. This is because the original MEX at position $$$p$$$ is no greater than the new MEX at position $$$p+1$$$, and the new MEX at the first position is at most $$$t$$$ smaller than the original MEX at position $$$i$$$.

Since $$$t \leq i$$$, placing $$$max$$$ at the first position is always an optimal strategy. Consequently, the remaining elements should be arranged in ascending order starting from 0, with any duplicate values moved to the end of the sequence.
2224C - Zhily and Bracket Swapping
2224C - Zhily and Bracket Swapping
If $$$a_i=b_i$$$, it doesn't matter; we ignore them. Otherwise, half of the $$$a_i$$$ should be '(', since there should be same number of '(' in $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$.

After that, the number of '(' and ')' in both $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ are determined. Thus, we just need to ensure for each prefix, the number of ')' is no more than '('. So we can just set $$$a_i$$$ = '(' if there are more ')' in $$$a$$$ before index $$$i$$$, and set $$$a_i$$$ = ')' otherwise.
We can see that it equals to simply set the odd indices of $$$i$$$ such that $$$a_i \neq b_i$$$ as $$$a_i$$$ = '(', vice versa. Just check if it's legal.
2224D - Zhily and Barknights
2224D - Zhily and Barknights
Fix $$$i \lt j$$$. After randomly permuting $$$b$$$, each ordered pair $$$(b_k, b_l)$$$ with $$$k \ne l$$$ is assigned to positions $$$(i, j)$$$ with probability $$$\frac{1}{n (n - 1)}$$$.
Therefore, the expected number of inversions equals
$$$$$$ \frac{1}{n (n - 1)}\sum_{i \lt j, k \ne l}[a_i b_k \gt a_j b_l]. $$$$$$
The square brackets in $$$[a_i b_k \gt a_j b_l]$$$ denote the Iverson bracket, an indicator function that evaluates to $$$1$$$ if the inequality is true and $$$0$$$ otherwise.
Solution 1:
Rewrite the inequality $$$a_i b_k \gt a_j b_l$$$ as $$$\frac{a_i}{a_j} \gt \frac{b_l}{b_k}.$$$

Compute all values $$$\frac{a_i}{a_j}$$$ for $$$i \lt j$$$, and all values $$$\frac{b_l}{b_k}$$$ for $$$k \ne l$$$. Sort both of these resulting sequences and use a two-pointer technique to count the number of valid pairs.

The time complexity depends on the sorting method. For example, using std::sort, we can achieve an $$$O(n^2\log n)$$$ approach, which can solve the problem within $$$0.6\text{s}$$$ and $$$50\text{MB}$$$.
Solution 2:
Consider all pairs $$$(i, k)$$$ and form a list of 2D elements $$$(a_i b_k, i)$$$.

Counting the number of quadruples $$$(i, j, k, l)$$$ with $$$i \lt j$$$ and $$$a_i b_k \gt a_j b_l$$$ is equivalent to counting dominating pairs among these elements. However, we must subtract the cases where $$$k = l$$$. The number of such cases is equal to $$$n$$$ times the inversion count of sequence $$$a$$$.
Dominating pairs can be counted using a Fenwick tree or merge sort in $$$O(n^2\log n)$$$ time, and this approach takes only $$$0.4\text{s}$$$.
2223C - Zhily and Signpost
2224E - Zhily and Signpost

Let $$$dis_u$$$ denote the total time from the root to node $$$u$$$. Each move $$$u \to son_{u,r}$$$ corresponds to a congruence equation $$$m + dis_u \equiv r\ (\mathrm{mod}\ d_u)$$$. Therefore, when we walk from the root to node $$$u$$$, we must satisfy a system of congruence equations. If it has a solution, we denote the solution by $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_u)$$$.
For node $$$u$$$ and its child $$$v$$$, we try to derive $$$M_v, R_v$$$ from $$$M_u, R_u$$$.

Specifically, we have $$$M_v = \mathrm{lcm}(M_u, d_u)$$$. Then $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_u)$$$ implies $$$m \equiv kM_u + R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_v),\ k \in [0,\frac{d_u}{\mathrm{gcd}(M_u, d_u)}-1]$$$. By enumerating all $$$k$$$ and computing the corresponding $$$r$$$, we can obtain the congruence equation for $$$s_{u,r}$$$. If some $$$r$$$ is not obtained, then the congruence equation corresponding to $$$s_{u,r}$$$ has no solution.
Next, we compress the depth of the tree.

Notice that if $$$d_u \mid M_u$$$, then $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_u)$$$ actually implies $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ d_u)$$$, so the child that $$$u$$$ can move to is unique. Then we can directly merge $$$u$$$ and this child into one node.

In the new tree obtained this way, every node $$$u$$$ satisfies $$$d_u \nmid M_u$$$. Then we have $$$M_v = \mathrm{lcm}(M_u, d_u) \ge 2M_u$$$. Let the upper bound of $$$m$$$ be $$$V = 10^{18}$$$. That is, any node $$$u$$$ with depth $$$\ge \log V + 2$$$ in this tree must satisfy $$$M_u \gt V$$$. Since the queries guarantee $$$m \le V$$$, there is at most one $$$m$$$ satisfying $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_u)$$$. This determines a unique leaf node reachable through $$$u$$$, so we can directly replace $$$u$$$ with this leaf node. Finally, the depth of this tree does not exceed $$$\log V + 2$$$, and the queries can be answered directly using the naive algorithm, with time complexity $$$O(q\log V)$$$.
We can prove that the preprocessing time complexity is $$$O(n)$$$. Therefore, the total time complexity is $$$O(n + q \log V)$$$.

Furthermore, we do not need to preprocess all $$$R_u$$$. We can perform the node-compression operation while processing the queries. When needed, we only need to use $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_u)$$$ to obtain the current node's $$$R_u$$$. The total time complexity is still $$$O(n + q \log V)$$$.
2223D - Zhily and Cycle
2223D - Zhily and Cycle

Assume there exists a Hamiltonian cycle, where point $$$i$$$ connects to $$$u_i$$$. Then, the edge $$$(i, u_i)$$$ can be split into two edges: $$$(i, a_i)$$$ and $$$(a_i, u_i)$$$, noting that $$$a_i \le u_i$$$ always holds.

Consider constructing a graph $$$G = (V, E)$$$, where $$$V = \{1, 2, \cdots, n\}$$$ and $$$E = \{(i, a_i) | 1 \le i \le n\}$$$. And if there exists a Hamiltonian cycle, there should exist an Eulerian circuit after adding some edges of the form $$$(a_i, u_i)$$$ to this graph. We only need to determine whether it is possible to add $$$n$$$ edges of the form $$$(a_i, u_i)$$$ to make $$$G$$$ an Eulerian graph.

Note that relaxing the restriction on adding edges does not affect the determination result. We can allow the addition of any number of edges $$$(u, v)$$$ satisfying $$$u \lt v$$$. Under such conditions, whether $$$G$$$ can become an Eulerian graph is equivalent to whether $$$G$$$ can become an Eulerian graph under the original conditions.

Consider how to determine whether there exists a scheme for adding edges. The conditions for an Eulerian graph are that the out-degree and in-degree of each vertex are equal and the graph is connected. Let the out-degree and in-degree of vertex $$$i$$$ be denoted as $$$out_i$$$ and $$$in_i$$$, respectively, and define $$$deg_i = out_i - in_i$$$. Consider the degree sequence of $$$G$$$: $$$deg_1, deg_2, \cdots, deg_n$$$. Each time, we can choose $$$i \lt j$$$ and update $$$deg_i \leftarrow deg_i + 1$$$ and $$$deg_j \leftarrow deg_j - 1$$$. Ultimately, we need to make all $$$deg_i$$$ equal to $$$0$$$ while ensuring the graph remains connected.

Let $$$sum_i = \sum_{u = 1}^{n} deg_u$$$. It is important to note that the condition for all $$$deg_i$$$ to be $$$0$$$ can be satisfied if and only if $$$\forall 1 \le i \le n, sum_i \le 0$$$. Therefore, we can add edges arbitrarily under this condition and see if we can make the graph connected.

Find all indices where $$$sum_i = 0$$$, denoting them as $$$t_0 = 0 \lt 1 \le t_1 \lt t_2 \lt \cdots \lt t_m = n$$$ (it is clear that $$$sum_n = 0$$$). Any edge we add cannot cross over $$$t_i$$$. Otherwise, if there exists $$$u \le t_i \lt v$$$ and we add $$$(u, v)$$$, then it must be the case that $$$sum_{t_i} \gt 0$$$, making it impossible to satisfy the degree constraints with any subsequent edge additions.

On the other hand, we can add all edges of the form $$$(i, i + 1)$$$ where $$$i \neq t_j$$$. If the graph is still not connected at this point, then it will never be possible to connect it regardless of how edges are added. Thus, we first add all such edges, and then greedily pair the remaining vertices with unbalanced in-degrees and out-degrees, adding no more than $$$3n$$$ edges in total.
If the above process is completed successfully, we will have obtained an Eulerian graph. We only need to find any Eulerian circuit in it to reconstruct a Hamiltonian cycle in the original graph.
The total complexity is $$$O(n)$$$
Also, there's an another solution given by gemini as follows.

We first sort $$$1, \cdots, n$$$ according to $$$a_i$$$ in increasing order, and denote the result sequence by $$$u_1, \cdots, u_n$$$, satisfying $$$a_{u_i} \lt a_{u_{i + 1}}$$$ for all $$$1\le i \lt n$$$. Then we simply link all the edges $$$(u_i, i)$$$. If the result doesn't meet the constraint $$$i \ge a_{u_i}$$$, it can be easily proved that the constraint can never be met and thus there isn't a Hamiltonian cycle in the graph.

And if the constraint is met, all left for us to do is to adjust the graph into one component. We check all pairs $$$(i, i + 1)$$$. If $$$i$$$ and $$$i + 1$$$ are not in the same component and $$$a_{u_{i + 1}} \le i$$$ (which means the following operation won't obey the constraint given by $$$a_i$$$), we alter the end points of $$$u_i$$$ and $$$u_{i + 1}$$$. Now let's prove that we can always find a Hamiltonian cycle after these operations if there is one in the graph.

Denote the node pointing to $$$i$$$ in the graph after the operations by $$$v_i$$$, and then we get the sequence $$$v_i$$$. If the graph still isn't connected, we denote the component containing $$$1$$$ with $$$S$$$ and all the other nodes as $$$T$$$($$$T = \{1, \cdots, n\} - S$$$), and they will form several consecutive segments on both the sequence $$$1, \cdots, n$$$ and $$$v_1, \cdots, v_n$$$(the indexes are corresponding). Since all valid operations have been done, the beginning of every segment will always satisfy that $$$a_{v_i} = i$$$. We claim that under these conditions there can never be a Hamiltonian cycle in the graph.

Consider how could we adjust the result to build a Hamiltonian cycle. To do this, we must build an edge pointing from $$$T$$$ to $$$S$$$, and let's assume it's $$$(v_i, j)$$$, where $$$v_i\in T, j\in S, i \lt j$$$. Consider which node will $$$v_j$$$ point to. It will be in either the segment containing $$$j$$$ or the following segments. If is the former, trace the augment path and the destination will always be in the following segments, which is the latter case. Thus, we will always have to build the edge $$$(v_j, k)$$$ where $$$v_j\in S, k\in T, j \lt k$$$. Doing the operation repeatedly and we will find conflict in the last segment.
So in summary, we can always find the Hamiltonian cycle if there is one. The whole algorithm can be implemented by DSU with time complexity $$$O(n\log n)$$$ bounding on the sort.
2223E - Zhily and Permutation
2223E - Zhily and Permutation
For convenience, we use $$$q$$$ to denote the operation count $$$m$$$ in the statement.

Brief: Through analysis of its properties, we can transform the maintenance of information regarding the left endpoint into a one-dimensional problem on a tree. During implementation, this transformation can be achieved during sweep line processes by maintaining sets using Binary Indexed Trees, resulting in a time complexity of $$$\Theta((n + q) \log n)$$$. After the transformation, the problem can be solved using various powerful data structures in $$$\Theta(n + q \log n)$$$ or using Heavy-Light Decomposition in $$$\Theta(n + q \log^2 n)$$$. This solution can be easily extended to handle online operations by introducing persistent data structures.

For convenience of notation, let $$$F = \{(l, r) \in ([0, n + 1] \cap \mathbb{N})^2 | r - l \gt 1\}$$$, and for $$$(l, r) \in F$$$ define $$$A(l, r) = \operatorname*{argmax} \{a_i\}_{i \in I}, B(l, r) = \operatorname*{argmax} \{b_j\}_{j \in I}, \varphi(l, r) = (\min(A(l, r), B(l, r)), \max(A(l, r), B(l, r)))$$$. Note that the equality between endpoint pairs $$$(1, 2) = (2, 3)$$$ does not hold.
We can consider enumerating $$$l$$$ from large to small, maintaining the state of $$$\varphi(l, \cdot)$$$.

Let $$$\{u_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|u_l|} = \{t \in (l, n] \cap \mathbb{N} | a_t = \max_{i = l + 1}^t a_i\}$$$ be the prefix maximum positions of $$$a$$$ in the current suffix $$$(l, n] \cap \mathbb{N}$$$, and similarly let $$$\{v_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|v_l|} = \{t \in (l, n] \cap \mathbb{N} | b_t = \max_{i = l + 1}^t b_i\}$$$. For convenience of notation, set $$$u_{l, |u_l| + 1} = v_{l, |v_l| + 1} = n + 1$$$. In particular, $$$u_{l - 1, 1} = v_{l - 1, 1} = l$$$, and $$$u_{l - 1, 2}, v_{l - 1, 2}$$$ denote the smallest index $$$k \in (l, n] \cap \mathbb{N}$$$ such that $$$a_k \gt a_l, b_k \gt b_l$$$, respectively (if no such $$$k$$$ exists, take $$$n + 1$$$).
From the definitions, we have:

Proposition 1: For $$$(l, r) \in F$$$, if $$$r \leqslant n$$$, $$$\left(\varphi(l, r) \neq \varphi(l, r + 1)\right) \Leftrightarrow \left(r \in \{u_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|u_l|} \cup \{v_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|v_l|}\right)$$$, and if $$$l \gt 0$$$, $$$\left(\varphi(l, r) \neq \varphi(l - 1, r) \right) \Leftrightarrow \left((u_{l - 1, 2} \geqslant r) \lor (v_{l - 1, 2} \geqslant r)\right)$$$.
Thus, we can obtain:

Proposition 2: For $$$(l, r) \in F$$$ satisfying $$$1 \leqslant l \lt r \leqslant n$$$, if $$$\varphi(l, r) = \varphi(l, r + 1)$$$, then $$$\varphi(l - 1, r) = \varphi(l - 1, r + 1)$$$; if $$$\varphi(l, r) = \varphi(l - 1, r)$$$, then $$$\varphi(l, r + 1) = \varphi(l - 1, r + 1)$$$.
It is also obvious that:

Proposition 3: For $$$(l, r) \in F$$$ satisfying $$$r - l \gt 2$$$, if $$$\varphi(l, r) \neq \varphi(l, r - 1)$$$ and $$$\varphi(l, r) \neq \varphi(l + 1, r)$$$, then $$$\varphi(l, r) = (l + 1, r - 1)$$$.
Propositions 4 to 7 can all be deduced from Propositions 2 and 3, independent of the specific content of $$$\varphi$$$.

Let $$$S = \{(l, r) \in F | (\exists (u, v) \in F)(\varphi(u, v) = (l, r))\}$$$. Then since $$$\varphi(S) \cap F \subseteq S$$$, it is obvious that after at least one transformation under $$$\varphi$$$, the endpoint pairs always lie in $$$S$$$. Since the first transformation under $$$\varphi$$$ is trivial to handle, we only need to focus on the endpoint pairs in $$$S$$$.
According to Propositions 2 and 3, we have:

Proposition 4: For $$$(x, y) \in S$$$, there exist $$$0 \leqslant L \lt x \leqslant y \lt R \leqslant n + 1$$$ such that $$$\left(\varphi(l, r) = (x, y)\right) \Leftrightarrow \left((l \in [L, x)) \land (r \in (y, R])\right)$$$.
According to Propositions 2 and 4, we have:
Proposition 5: For $$$(x, y) \in S$$$, $$$\varphi(x, y), \varphi(x - 1, y), \varphi(x, y + 1), \varphi(x - 1, y + 1)$$$ are pairwise distinct.
According to Propositions 4 and 5, we have:
Proposition 6: For $$$(l, r) \in S$$$, there is at most one $$$(x, y) \in S$$$ such that $$$\varphi(x, y) = (l, r)$$$.
In other words, if we connect elements of $$$S$$$ by directed edges according to the transformation under $$$\varphi$$$, then $$$S$$$ consists of several chains.

These chains can be easily ordered according to the endpoint pairs of the empty intervals obtained by applying $$$\varphi$$$ once more to the chain tails. By mathematical induction, it is easy to prove that:

Proposition 7: There exists a numbering function $$$\psi: F \to \mathbb{N}$$$ such that for $$$(l, r) \in F$$$, if $$$\varphi(l, r) \in F$$$ then $$$\psi(l, r) = \psi(\varphi(l, r))$$$; and if $$$(l, r), (x, y) \in F$$$ satisfy $$$l \leqslant x$$$ and $$$r \leqslant y$$$, then $$$\psi(l, r) \leqslant \psi(x, y)$$$.

Since Propositions 2 and 3 are local properties, the above property analysis from Proposition 2 to Proposition 7 can also be directly observed during the sweep line process. They can also be directly proved using other methods.

During the sweep line process, for disappearances of right endpoints from $$$\{u_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|u_l|} \cup \{v_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|v_l|}$$$, they are associated with the termination of a chain; similarly at endpoint pairs $$$(l, \max(u_{l, 2}, v_{l, 2})) \notin S$$$. According to Proposition 7, the rank of the terminated chain is the same as the rank of the disappearing endpoint. Hence we can separately maintain the set of current non-terminated chains.
Thus, for each left endpoint, during the sweep line we process an interval of chains such that any chain in this interval that has not terminated before must contain this left endpoint.
All sets can be maintained using binary indexed trees, and thus the time complexity of the above sweep line process is $$$\Theta(n \log n)$$$.

We can perform a second sweep line process in the order of the chains, with point insertions of left endpoints, so we can maintain the set of left endpoints for each chain in $$$\Theta(n \log n)$$$ time, and for each query compute the final interval reached within $$$k$$$ iterations of $$$\operatorname{next}$$$ in $$$\Theta(\log n)$$$ time.

If the queried information is commutative and associative, then the problem can be solved directly using 2D orthogonal range counting methods. However, when a generalized semigroup operation rather than the general addition is utilized, we can construct another $$$\varphi'$$$ that also satisfies Propositions 2 and 3, such that under the APSP hypothesis and when $$$q = \Theta(n)$$$, the corresponding problem cannot be solved in $$$O(n^{1.5-\varepsilon})$$$ time, where $$$\varepsilon$$$ is any positive constant. In other words, we need more properties concerning $$$\varphi$$$ than those given in Propositions 2 to 7 to solve the problem when utilizing generalized semigroup operations (or the semigroup operation in the statement).
We prove the following property independently of Propositions 2 and 3:
Proposition 8: If for $$$(r, x), (s, y), (t, z)\in F$$$, we have $$$r \lt t \lt s$$$, $$$(t, z) \in S$$$ and $$$\varphi(r, x) = (s, y)$$$, then $$$z \leqslant s$$$.

From $$$\varphi(r, x) = (s, y)$$$, we have either $$$s = A(r, x)$$$ or $$$s = B(r, x)$$$; consider the former case without loss of generality. Since $$$(t, z) \in S$$$, let $$$(t, z) = \varphi(\alpha, \beta)$$$, then $$$t = A(\alpha, \beta)$$$ or $$$t = B(\alpha, \beta)$$$.

If $$$t = A(\alpha, \beta)$$$, then because $$$t \in (r, s) \subseteq (r, x)$$$ and $$$s = A(r, x)$$$, we have $$$a_s \geqslant a_t$$$, and for $$$A(\alpha, \beta) = t$$$ to hold, we must have $$$s \geqslant \beta \gt z$$$.

If $$$t = B(\alpha, \beta)$$$, then similarly $$$b_y \geqslant b_t$$$ and $$$y \geqslant \beta$$$, and since $$$\alpha \lt t \lt s$$$ and for $$$u \in (t, y)$$$ we have $$$a_u \lt a_t$$$, we must have $$$z = A(\alpha, \beta) \leqslant s$$$.
Thus we must have $$$z \leqslant s$$$.
Then it immediately follows that for $$$(d, w) = \varphi(t, z)$$$ we have $$$d \lt z \leqslant s$$$.
Therefore:
Proposition 9: The paths of left endpoints in $$$S$$$ under the transformation of $$$\varphi$$$ are on a forest. (With a virtual root, we get a tree.)
In fact, during the problem preparation, this conclusion is naturally obtained from a more complex but powerful structure; for simplicity, we now consider the direct proof above.
In the first sweep line process, we can directly process which new left endpoints a left endpoint in $$$S$$$ can reach via $$$\varphi$$$. So the tree can be determined.
The endpoints of the tree paths can also be determined, so we only need to solve the problem of point updates and path sum queries on the tree.

The time complexity is $$$\Theta((n + q) \log n)$$$, and the space complexity of the offline algorithm is $$$\Theta(n + q)$$$. Since the sweep line process is independent of updates, we can extend it to an online algorithm using persistent segment trees, in which case the space complexity becomes $$$\Theta(n \log n)$$$.

The standard solution runs in 546ms at its slowest point on Polygon. For the Heavy-Light Decomposition implementation, since we have not yet constructed targeted adversarial data, the slowest point is currently 510ms. The time limit 2.5s was set by the coordinator after considering several other potential solutions.

Due to slight time constraints during preparation, the design of this problem still has certain shortcomings (though they did not manifest during the contest). We hope for your understanding and forgiveness.
2223F - Zhily and Colorful Strings
2223F - Zhily and Colorful Strings
Let $$$n_i = k_i d_i$$$, where $$$k_i$$$ is a non-negative integer; otherwise, there is no solution.
We first consider how to check if a string is valid. Note that we can remove the characters in any order, while it will not change the validity.

Therefore, we can use a stack storing triples like $$$(i, j, t)$$$ meaning there remain $$$t$$$ consecutive characters in the $$$j$$$-th color of the $$$i$$$-th type. For a new character, we consider whether it will push or pop the top, or let the $$$t$$$ of the top increase by $$$1$$$.

Note that this procedure forms a matching structure like a bracket sequence: $$$d_i$$$ characters of the $$$i$$$-th type we removed at once are like a tuple of brackets containing $$$d_i-1$$$ substrings among them.

Now, to count the result, we first consider the bracket structure and then count the coloring ways in which the stack-using procedure can form it. This requires that each bracket should not be the same kind and the same color as the element below in the stack.
For convenience, we can calculate the sum of the valid coloring probabilities of all bracket sequences and then multiply by $$$c_1^{k_1} c_2^{k_2} \dots c_m^{k_m}$$$. Let $$$q_i = \frac1{c_i}$$$.
Let $$$F_i(\mathbf x)$$$ be the number of bracket sequences with an outermost bracket that is of the $$$i$$$-th type. We can derive the equation:
This means that in the $$$d_i$$$ brackets, we can insert a bracket sequence in the $$$d_i-1$$$ gaps, but we need to exclude the cases where they are the same color.
To apply the multivariate Lagrange inversion, we rearrange it into a suitable form:

$$$$$$ \begin{aligned} G_i(\mathbf x) &= \frac1{(1-x_1-\dots-x_m+q_ix_i)^{d_i-1}} \\ &= \frac1{(1-x_1-\dots-x_m)^{d_i-1}\left(1+\frac{q_ix_i}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m}\right)^{d_i-1}} \\ F_i(\mathbf x) &= x_i G_i(\mathbf F) \\ \frac{x_j}{G_i(\mathbf x)} \frac{\partial G_i(\mathbf x)}{\partial x_j} &= \frac{(d_i-1)(1-[i=j]q_i) x_j}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m+q_ix_i} \\ &= (d_i-1)(1-[i=j]q_i) \frac{x_j}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m} \frac1{1+\frac{q_ix_i}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m}}\\ H(\mathbf x) &= \frac1{1-x_1-\dots-x_m} \end{aligned} $$$$$$
We want to find
$$$$$$ [\mathbf x^{\mathbf k}] H(\mathbf F) = [\mathbf x^{\mathbf k}] H \mathbf G^{\mathbf k} \left\Vert[i=j]-\frac{x_j}{G_i(\mathbf x)} \frac{\partial G_i(\mathbf x)}{\partial x_j}\right\Vert $$$$$$
Notice that the expression on the right side is of the form
$$$$$$ [\mathbf x^{\mathbf k}] \frac1{(1-x_1-\dots-x_m)^{1+\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf d-\mathbf 1)}} P\left(\frac{x_1}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m},\dots,\frac{x_m}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m}\right) $$$$$$
We first calculate $$$P(t_1,t_2,\dots,t_m)$$$. It should be

$$$$$$ \begin{aligned} P &= \prod_{i=1}^m \frac1{(1+q_it_i)^{k_i(d_i-1)}} \cdot \left\Vert[i=j]-(d_i-1)(1-[i=j]q_i)\frac{t_j}{1+q_it_i}\right\Vert \\ &= \prod_{i=1}^m \frac1{(1+q_it_i)^{k_i(d_i-1)+1}} \cdot \left\Vert[i=j](1+d_iq_it_i)-(d_i-1)t_j\right\Vert \\ &= \prod_{i=1}^m \frac1{(1+q_it_i)^{k_i(d_i-1)+1}} \cdot \left(1-\sum_{i=1}^m \frac{(d_i-1)t_i}{1+d_iq_it_i}\right) \cdot \prod_{i=1}^m (1+d_iq_it_i) \\ &= [u^1] (1+u)\prod_{i=1}^m \frac{1+d_iq_it_i-(d_i-1)ut_i}{(1+q_it_i)^{k_i(d_i-1)+1}} \end{aligned} $$$$$$
The third equality holds because for invertible matrices $$$\mathbf A, \mathbf W$$$, we have
$$$$$$ \det(\mathbf A + \mathbf U\mathbf W\mathbf V) = \det(\mathbf W^{-1} + \mathbf V\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf U) \det(\mathbf W) \det(\mathbf A) $$$$$$
which can be simply proven using block matrices.
Next, we consider what contribution an item $$$\mathbf t^{\mathbf e}$$$ in $$$P(\mathbf t)$$$ will bring to the answer:

$$$$$$ [\mathbf x^{\mathbf k-\mathbf e}] \frac1{(1-x_1-\dots-x_m)^{1+\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf d-\mathbf 1)+\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf 1}} = \binom{\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf d}{\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf d-\mathbf 1)+\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf 1,k_1-e_1,k_2-e_2,\dots,k_m-e_m} $$$$$$
Thus, we only care about $$$\sum e_i$$$ and $$$\prod \frac1{(k_i-e_i)!}$$$.

Now considering the comprehensive calculation, note that we have already organized $$$P$$$ into a form where each variable is independent, so we can introduce a dummy variable $$$w$$$ to measure $$$\sum e_i$$$:

$$$$$$ \sum_{s\ge 0} \frac{(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf d)!}{(\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf d-1)+s)!}[w^s] \left([u^1](1+u)\prod_{i=1}^m \sum_{e=0}^{k_i} \frac{w^e}{(k_i-e)!} \cdot [t_i^e] \frac{1+d_iq_it_i-(d_i-1)ut_i}{(1+q_it_i)^{k_i(d_i-1)+1}}\right) $$$$$$
Of course, we also need to multiply by $$$\mathbf c^{\mathbf k}$$$
